In lower Puna, vacant lots averaged about $28,500 in early 2019, compared to about $252,000 in South Hilo. In a 2024 insurance-industry report, a lawmaker pointed out that these lava hazard zones offer an affordable way to live in Hawaii. On the other side, the president of an insurers' council argued that prices should reflect risk, and after an eruption like 2018, public recovery funds—mostly from the federal government—rebuild the main public roads, while private subdivision owners maintain their own gravel lanes and catch rainwater from their roofs. Should people be free to build where lava has been because it offers affordable living, or should the cost of land and insurance reflect the full risk? Which side do you lean toward, and why? And tell us where you're watching from, and who maintains the road outside your home. 👇
